learn: Why sequence-to-sequence tasks need an encoder–decoder, and its fixed-vector bottleneck
The RNN recurrence, worked on 'I don't like NLP'
Vanishing gradients and how LSTM gates and the cell state help
Attention as soft alignment, with a worked context vector
Transformer self-attention: queries, keys, values and scaling
Multi-head attention, padding and look-ahead masks, residual connections, LayerNorm and feed-forward layers
BERT: contextual embeddings, masked language modelling, next-sentence prediction and fine-tuning
intro.why: This is the path from early neural sequence models to the architecture behind every modern language model. Understanding the bottleneck, vanishing gradients and attention explains why Transformers replaced RNNs, and BERT shows the pre-train-then-fine-tune recipe used across NLP.
prereq: Session M8 (LSTM gates, self-attention for tagging)

symbols: RNN hidden state at step t

sections.title: Encoder–decoder and the bottleneck
sections.plain: Read the whole input into a summary, then generate the output from that summary; one fixed summary can't hold everything.
sections.body:
Translation can't be word-for-word: "I love you" → "Je t'aime", not "Je aime tu"; words reorder, merge and split. The encoder–decoder (sequence-to-sequence) architecture reads the source with an encoder into a context vector and a decoder generates the target word by word from it (like zipping a file and unzipping it in another language).

In the classic RNN version the context is the encoder's final hidden state: a fixed size (e.g. 256 numbers) whatever the input length. Long sentences must be compressed into the same space, so details are lost and quality drops with length: the bottleneck that attention removes.

sections.title: The RNN recurrence
sections.plain: Update a running memory with each word, reusing the same weights at every step.
sections.body:
$$h_t = \tanh(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)$$

Like adding drops of colour to a glass of water: each word tints the running mixture, and the final colour reflects the whole sequence (with recent drops more visible). The same $W_h, W_x$ are shared across time, so the network handles any length; unrolled in time it is a deep network with tied weights.

Worked ("I don't like NLP", I = [1, 0], don't = [0, −1], like = [1, 1], NLP = [−1, 1]; $W_h = 0.5I$, $W_x = I$, b = 0, $h_0$ = 0):

  • h₁ = tanh([1, 0]) = [0.762, 0].
  • h₂ = tanh(0.5·[0.762, 0] + [0, −1]) = tanh([0.381, −1]) = [0.363, −0.762].
  • h₃ = tanh([0.182 + 1, −0.381 + 1]) = [0.828, 0.551]; h₄ = [−0.527, 0.855].

sections.title: Vanishing gradients and LSTMs
sections.plain: Learning signals fade over many steps; LSTMs add a protected memory lane controlled by gates.
sections.body:
Backpropagation through time multiplies one factor per step ($W_h$ times the tanh slope). If those factors are below 1 the gradient shrinks exponentially (≈ 0.21 per step gives 10⁻¹³ after 20 steps): vanishing gradients, like a message fading in a game of telephone. The network then can't learn long-distance dependencies such as agreement in "The cats that the dog chased yesterday are …". Factors above 1 cause exploding gradients (fixed by clipping).

The LSTM adds a cell state $C_t$, a conveyor belt updated by addition and controlled by gates:

$$f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f),\ i_t = \sigma(\cdot),\ \tilde C_t = \tanh(\cdot),\ C_t = f_t C_{t-1} + i_t\tilde C_t,\ o_t = \sigma(\cdot),\ h_t = o_t\tanh(C_t)$$

When the forget gate stays near 1 and the input gate near 0, information (and gradient) passes along unchanged for many steps.

sections.title: Attention: a worked alignment
sections.plain: At each output step, look back at all input positions and take a weighted mix of the relevant ones.
sections.body:
Instead of one fixed context, the decoder computes a fresh context at every step, focusing a "spotlight" on the relevant source words:

$$e_i = s_t\cdot h_i,\qquad \alpha_i = \frac{\exp(e_i)}{\sum_j\exp(e_j)},\qquad c_t = \sum_i \alpha_i h_i$$

Worked: decoder state $s_t$ = [1, 0]; encoder states h₁ ("bank") = [1, 1], h₂ ("river") = [0, 1]. Scores e₁ = 1, e₂ = 0; e¹ + e⁰ ≈ 3.718; α₁ ≈ 0.73, α₂ ≈ 0.27; $c_t$ = 0.73·[1, 1] + 0.27·[0, 1] = [0.73, 1.00].

This is soft alignment: every source word contributes a fraction, learned end-to-end, instead of a hard one-to-one mapping (one word can map to several, and its meaning can depend on context: French "poste" can be mail or a job). Attention also makes models more interpretable, as weights show which source words were used.

sections.title: Transformer self-attention
sections.plain: Every word looks at every other word in the same sentence at once; no recurrence needed.
sections.body:
The Transformer ("Attention Is All You Need", 2017) drops recurrence. RNNs are sequential (step 10 waits for step 9); self-attention computes all positions in parallel. Each token's embedding is projected into a query (what am I looking for?), key (what do I contain?) and value (what do I pass on?), like searching a library catalogue:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V$$

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps dot products from growing with dimension and saturating the softmax. In "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", a trained head links "it" to "animal"; change "tired" to "wide" and it links to "street". Cost is O(n²) in sequence length, but any two positions are one step apart.

sections.title: Multi-head attention, masks and residual blocks
sections.plain: Run several attention heads side by side, hide what shouldn't be seen, and wrap each sub-layer with a shortcut and normalisation.
sections.body:
$$\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W^O,\quad \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)$$

Each head has its own projections and can specialise (syntax, coreference, position), like a committee whose members' notes are combined. Then a position-wise feed-forward network processes each token independently (in the original model 512 → 2048 → 512 with ReLU).

Masks: a padding mask stops attention to [PAD] tokens added to equalise batch lengths; a look-ahead (causal) mask in the decoder hides future positions so generation can't cheat. Masked scores are set to −∞ before softmax.

Every sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)): residual connections give gradients a direct path through deep stacks, and layer normalisation keeps activations well scaled. The original encoder and decoder each stack six such blocks; the decoder adds cross-attention over encoder outputs.

sections.title: Positional encodings
sections.plain: Attention ignores order, so add a position signal to every word vector.
sections.body:
Self-attention is permutation-invariant: shuffle the words and each output is just shuffled. To inject order, add a positional encoding to each input embedding:

$$PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big),\qquad PE(pos, 2i+1) = \cos\Big(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\Big)$$

Different dimensions oscillate at different frequencies, like the second, minute and hour hands of a clock: together they give each position a unique pattern. PE(pos + k) is a linear function (rotation) of PE(pos), so relative positions are easy to learn, and the formula extends to lengths not seen in training. With d = 8: PE(0) = [0, 1, 0, 1, …], PE(1) = [0.841, 0.540, 0.100, 0.995, …]; nearby positions have larger dot products (PE(1)·PE(2) = 3.54 vs PE(1)·PE(10) = 1.71). Many later models learn position embeddings or use relative/rotary schemes instead.

sections.title: BERT: contextual embeddings and pre-training
sections.plain: A stack of Transformer encoders trained to fill in blanks using both sides of the context, then adapted to many tasks.
sections.body:
Static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) give "bank" one vector whether by the river or in finance. Contextual embeddings compute a vector for each occurrence from its sentence. BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a stack of Transformer encoders (12 layers in BERT-base) pre-trained on large text with two objectives:

  • Masked language modelling: select 15% of tokens (80% replaced by [MASK], 10% by a random token, 10% unchanged) and predict the originals from both sides: "The [MASK] sat on the [MASK]" → cat, mat. Left-to-right language models can't use the right context this way.
  • Next sentence prediction: is sentence B the real continuation of A? ("The man went to the store." + "He bought a gallon of milk." → true; + "Penguins are flightless birds." → false.) Later models (RoBERTa) found NSP unnecessary.

Fine-tuning adds a small task-specific head (classification from the [CLS] token, a tag per token, start/end positions for question answering) and trains briefly on labelled data: one pre-trained model, many tasks, like a Swiss Army knife. Decoder-only models (GPT family) instead pre-train left-to-right for generation.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Bahdanau vs Luong attention: additive (small network) vs multiplicative (dot-product) scoring.
  • Teacher forcing: during training the decoder is fed the gold previous word, not its own guess.
  • Attention ≠ explanation: weights show information flow but aren't a full account of a model's reasoning.
  • Long contexts: O(n²) attention motivates sparse, linear and memory-efficient variants.

code.title: RNN states, vanishing gradients and an attention step
code.explain: Runs the RNN over 'I don't like NLP' (h₁ = [0.762, 0], h₂ = [0.363, −0.762], h₃ = [0.828, 0.551], h₄ = [−0.527, 0.855]), shows how a per-step factor of ≈ 0.21 shrinks gradients to 10⁻¹³ over 20 steps, and computes the bank/river attention (0.73/0.27, context [0.73, 1.00]).
mistakes: Using a new weight matrix per step.
code.code:
"""An RNN over 'I don't like NLP', vanishing gradients, and one step of encoder-decoder attention."""
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

X = {"I": [1, 0], "don't": [0, -1], "like": [1, 1], "NLP": [-1, 1]}
Wh, Wx, b = 0.5 * np.eye(2), np.eye(2), np.zeros(2)
h = np.zeros(2)
for w, x in X.items():
    h = np.tanh(Wh @ h + Wx @ np.array(x) + b)
    print(f"after {w!r:8s} h = {h}")
print("final h is the whole sentence squeezed into", h.size, "numbers (the encoder bottleneck)")

# Vanishing gradient: d h_T / d h_1 is a product of T-1 Jacobians (here scalar for intuition)
for T in (5, 20, 50):
    print(f"T={T:2d}: 0.5 * tanh' ~ 0.5*0.42 per step -> gradient factor {(0.5*0.42)**(T-1):.2e}")

# Attention: decoder state s, encoder states for 'bank' and 'river'
s = np.array([1, 0]); H = {"bank": np.array([1, 1]), "river": np.array([0, 1])}
e = np.array([s @ v for v in H.values()]); a = np.exp(e) / np.exp(e).sum()
c = sum(w * v for w, v in zip(a, H.values()))
print("scores", e, "weights", a.round(2), "context", c.round(2))

code.title: Transformer building blocks and BERT masking
code.explain: Implements scaled dot-product attention with and without a causal mask, two heads concatenated with W^O, residual + LayerNorm and a feed-forward layer, sinusoidal positional encodings with similarity checks, and BERT's 15% / 80-10-10 masking.
mistakes: Masking after softmax instead of before.
code.notes: Random weights; shapes and mechanics, not a trained model.
code.code:
"""Scaled dot-product self-attention with a causal mask, multi-head concat, residual + LayerNorm,
sinusoidal positional encodings, and BERT-style masking."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    if mask is not None: S = np.where(mask, S, -1e9)
    A = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True)); A /= A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return A @ V, A

X = rng.normal(size=(4, 8))                    # 4 tokens, d_model = 8
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(8, 8)) / np.sqrt(8) for _ in range(3))
out, A = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)
print("attention weights (rows sum to 1):\n", A, "\nrow sums", A.sum(1))
causal = np.tril(np.ones((4, 4), bool))
_, Ac = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv, causal)
print("with look-ahead mask (decoder):\n", Ac)

# two heads of size 4, concatenated and projected by W_O
heads = [attention(X @ Wq[:, i*4:(i+1)*4], X @ Wk[:, i*4:(i+1)*4], X @ Wv[:, i*4:(i+1)*4])[0] for i in range(2)]
WO = rng.normal(size=(8, 8)) / np.sqrt(8)
mh = np.concatenate(heads, 1) @ WO
ln = lambda z: (z - z.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / z.std(1, keepdims=True)
Y = ln(X + mh)                                   # residual + LayerNorm
FFN = lambda z: np.maximum(0, z @ rng.normal(size=(8, 32)) / 3) @ rng.normal(size=(32, 8)) / 6  # 8 -> 32 -> 8 (paper: 512 -> 2048 -> 512)
Z = ln(Y + FFN(Y))
print("block output shape", Z.shape, "| per-token mean ~0, std ~1:", Z.mean(1).round(2), Z.std(1).round(2))

# sinusoidal positional encodings
def pe(pos, d=8):
    i = np.arange(d // 2)
    ang = pos / 10000 ** (2 * i / d)
    v = np.empty(d); v[0::2] = np.sin(ang); v[1::2] = np.cos(ang); return v
for p in (0, 1, 2, 10):
    print(f"PE(pos={p:2d}) =", pe(p))
print("dot(PE1,PE2) =", round(pe(1) @ pe(2), 3), " dot(PE1,PE10) =", round(pe(1) @ pe(10), 3), "(nearby positions are more similar)")

# BERT masked-LM corruption: choose 15% of tokens; 80% [MASK], 10% random, 10% unchanged
toks = "the cat sat on the mat because it was tired and wanted to sleep all afternoon".split()
r = np.random.default_rng(3); chosen = r.random(len(toks)) < 0.15; outp = []
for t, c in zip(toks, chosen):
    if not c: outp.append(t); continue
    u = r.random(); outp.append("[MASK]" if u < 0.8 else (r.choice(toks) if u < 0.9 else t) + "*")
print("input :", " ".join(toks)); print("masked:", " ".join(outp), f"({chosen.sum()} of {len(toks)} chosen)")
